cells.tense: The ending is real and you are still standing among the people it touched.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: When a plan, a person, or an opening shows up, meet it that same day, not three days later.
cells.core:
Something in your life with people has finished, and you're not pretending otherwise. You can be among them and still know the season turned. That's why contact doesn't have to be strained — you're not dragging a closed thing forward to prove you cared. The connection is real; the old shape of it is done.

What's here now is what to stay with. Each time you're with someone, take it as it comes rather than continuing a version of it you've already lived. There's likely something at the edge of your week, half-arrived, waiting for you to look at it properly. When it shows — a message, an offer, a question — take it that day, not after you've rehearsed it. You'll keep the person and lose the performance.
cells.sheetLine: The season turned. The people are still here.
cells.verb: completing what is done and letting the making carry forward
cells.place: among people, staying in living contact

cells.tense: You have already written the ending of something that is still in the middle of being lived.
cells.act: let this moment be a fresh entry, not a continuation
cells.ask: Take each conversation this week as if you were having it for the first time, and don't decide in advance where it ends.
cells.core:
You've called it done ahead of time. There's a person or a situation where the ending has been declared — at least in your own head — while the actual thing is still moving. Bracing for the close makes you manage it, and the managing is doing the damage: you're not in the conversation, you're at the end of it, looking back.

Try meeting it with nothing prepared. Take each moment with people as freshly given, not as chapter eleven of a book you've already finished. No pre-decided conclusion. It's possible you're right about where it's headed — but arriving there early costs you the middle, which is where the whole thing is. The current is slower than your forecast.
cells.sheetLine: You finished it in your head. It hasn't finished.
cells.verb: completing what is done and letting the making carry forward
cells.place: among people, staying in living contact

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you while you weren't looking.
cells.act: open the door to the next thing on time, not early
cells.ask: Where you've been keeping something in motion past its end, simply stop moving it. Let it rest there.
cells.core:
You keep things alive past their finish and call it loyalty or patience. Something has ended with people — a version of a friendship, a way of being close, a shared project — and you're still tending it, still circling it, still waiting to find out what it was. Seeking the answer has become the answer. The door is behind you and your hand is on it.

What's needed isn't more effort. Let it rest. Not to close it by force, just to stop holding it up. What's arriving for you comes through the open side, not the one you're pushing. Put the weight down and see what's already on the other side of it.
cells.sheetLine: The door closed. Your hand is still on it.
cells.verb: completing what is done and letting the making carry forward
cells.place: among people, staying in living contact

cells.tense: You are writing something you still call provisional, and the ending already happened.
cells.act: surrender the outcome and keep the act
cells.ask: With one person, keep showing up to what you do together, and drop what you need it to come to.
cells.core:
You don't know which of your cycles has closed. Some part of your life with people has finished and you're still treating it as ongoing — or you've walked away from something whose last note hasn't quite landed. The lines are there, you just can't find where one thing ended and the next began. That's not a flaw; it's the ordinary blur of living among people.

Keep the contact and stop steering it. With one person, keep showing up to the thing you actually do together and let go of what you need it to produce. Releasing the outcome isn't abandoning them — it's making room. What's genuinely over will settle without your grip, and what isn't will show itself. Your name is still on the work.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that a specific cycle has actually closed in the person's life — the record carries only where authorship stands, not the state of any relationship. The reader could say 'nothing has ended, it's still going' and still use every cell, since each asks for present-moment meeting rather than a verdict on what is over. The asks survive being wrong because they are practices of noticing and release, not declarations about a relationship. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'the cycle closes' — I've kept completion as something the person recognises, not something I announce.
